speechtext:
Mr. Speaker,
I wanted to see today's Hansard before I brought up a point of order which I think is of some importance to us on this side of the House, and I am sure the Government would concur.
Yesterday at the beginning of the sitting, the Parliamentary Secretary to the Deputy Prime Minister and House Leader (Mr. Lewis) rose in his place to move what we all knew to be a dilatory motion. He moved that we proceed to Orders of the Day. At the time, as far as I know, there was no question before the House to be debated, yet he was allowed to put his dilatory motion and it was voted on and, of course, carried.
I would like to make sure the Chair understands my point. I am not questioning the Chair's acceptance of the motion. What I do question was the Parliamentary Secretary's right to take the floor when there was nothing before us to move a dilatory motion which prevented many of us from tabling petitions and doing the regular things we do under Routine Proceedings.
I would give notice to the Chair today that I would like this matter to be discussed, possibly in the Chamber, so that we do not have a repetition of what happened yesterday, a dilatory motion being used by the Government to do certain things. We all know that the Government has many tools at hand to cut off debate, to adjourn the House or to do all kinds of other things. In my view, the Government is utilizing its powers to push too far the importance of its wish to get the Government's business done, and is using the rules badly in so doing.

speakeroldname: Mr. Doug Lewis (Parliamentary Secretary to Deputy Prime Minister and President of the Privy Council):
subtopic: DAILY ROUTINE OF BUSINESS-ACCEPTABILITY OF MOTION AT COMMENCEMENT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on the same point of order. I think it is common practice that once prayers are finished, your remark is: "Let the doors be opened". I felt that that was an indication to the House that the business of the House could proceed. Under daily Routine Proceedings, I would suggest, Sir, that a motion to move to Orders of the Day is in order. There does not have to be a question before the House, so I moved at that time to proceed directly to Government Orders in order that the business of the House which had not been able to proceed on three preceding days might proceed.
A comment has been made about the ability of Hon. Members to present petitions. I know that my hon. friend who is a student of the House rules would be the first to tell the Chair that there are two ways to bring a petition to the attention of the Speaker. There is the method used when petitions are presented under the daily Routine Proceedings and there is also the method of tabling petitions, a method which does not require that one stand in one's place to make a lengthy presentation. Many Hon. Members, with the interests of the nation at heart, table petitions in this much more businesslike way. I suggest, Sir, that by moving to Orders of the Day, in no way were we preventing any Member from presenting a petition to the Speaker since there is another method of doing so.
In closing, I would simply say that in my copies of the Projected Order of Business and the Order Paper and Notices, it indicates this day's order of business. I think Routine Proceedings should include the right to make a motion. I suggest that if my hon. friend wants to make the same motion, that we proceed to Orders of the Day, we would be able to assist him in that.

speechtext: The House resumed from Monday, February 9, 1987, consideration of the motion of Mr. Crosbie that Bill C-19, an Act respecting motor vehicle transport by extra-provincial undertakings, be read the second time and referred to the Standing Committee on Transport; and the motion of Mr. Lewis (p. 3220).

subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, let me begin my remarks on Bill C-19, the Government's proposed deregulation of the trucking industry, by pointing out that the Government is throwing out the baby with the bath water. The Government could have chosen a number of alternatives to deal with the trucking industry. It could abandon regulation, as it has done with this legislation; it could decide no change is necessary and keep the status quo\ or it could have taken a moderate approach to the regulation of the trucking industry and make constructive reforms that could benefit both the shippers and the trucking industry while modernizing the regulatory regime. However, the Government has decided to abandon regulation.

Mr. Speaker, I want to point out that the decision of the Government was to abandon the regulatory system. The Government had several options. It could have decided, as it did, to abandon the regulatory system, or else it could have maintained that the existing system was marvelous and did not require any change or Finally, it could approach the regulatory system as in need of reform. For my part, I believe that a constructive reform to update the regulatory system as it applies to the trucking industry would have been the best approach. However, the Government decided to throw away the baby with the bathwater. This is a destructive approach.
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986

There are three aspects of this Bill on which I want to comment. They are safety, the impact of deregulation on Manitoba, since I am a representative of Manitoba, and the over-all economic impact of abandoning regulation in the trucking industry.
The Government has proposed to remove regulation of the trucking industry to make it a wide open free market in which the strongest will survive and the fastest will win the race. Consequently, truckers will push themselves to the limit and perhaps beyond because they will be living from day to day and load to load. This lack of security will cause them to continue driving even when they are exhausted.
In the United States this question of fatigue has been raised as a result of their experience with a deregulated environment. I have a report by a foundation study on truck driver fatigue and highway accidents which indicates a shockingly high number of fatigue related big truck accidents. Let me cite some of those statistics for the record. First, 60 per cent of the 231 accidents studied involved fatigue. Second, the fatigue factor was shown to be three times greater than accident reports indicated. Third, 49 of the 231 accidents studied involved fatalities; 16 truck occupants and 33 occupants of other vehicles. Fourth, 63 per cent of the truck occupant fatalities occurred in fatigue related accidents. Fifth, 6.5 per cent of the drivers of heavy truck are estimated to be driving more than 16 consecutive hours, which is the equivalent of two eight-hour work shifts. Finally, one out of every three truck drivers is driving beyond the limit of the Federal Bureau of Motor Carrier Safety which is recommended at 10 hours per day.
I am giving these statistics to show that fatigue plays a very significant part in the safety of the trucking industry. It will play an even greater role if the trucking industry no longer operates in a regulated environment. The competition will force truckers to push themselves further while attempting to survive on a day-to-day basis. The approach of abandoning regulation in the trucking industry raises serious questions about safety, which the Government should consider before it proceeds any further with this legislation.
Another aspect of the whole question of abandoning the regulatory regime in the trucking industry has to do with its regional impact. I am particularly concerned about what this means for Manitoba. Manitoba has been hit hard by the Government on a number of occasions. When the Government reduced the transfers for education and health care, provinces like Manitoba were the hardest hit. It is not the first time the Government has taken some action which hurt Manitobans. I would like to read an excerpt from an article in The Ottawa Citizen on October 22, 1985:
Manitoba stands to lose more than most provinces if reform of the trucking industry fails to safeguard domestic routes from competition by giant United States firms,-

February 10, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
That was said by Roily Painchaud, President of the Manitoba Trucking Association. Mr. Painchaud went on to say:
Eight of Canada's 14 largest trucking firms are based in Winnipeg and more than 400 local trucking firms employ about 10,000 Manitobans.
He noted that hundreds of jobs could be lost through imprudent regulatory change. We are talking about an industry which employs 10,000 Manitobans in a province with a population of one million people. This is a very significant industry for Manitoba. It affects the employment of a great number of Manitobans. The Manitoba trucking industry is telling us to watch out. It has put out the warning signals. It is saying, "Wake up. If you go ahead with this abandonment of the regulation of the trucking industry, you are threatening jobs which exist in Manitoba". They indicate that hundreds of jobs could be lost to Manitoba.
I wanted to bring those facts to the attention of the Government. While I have not much hope it will listen, we will have at least put it on the record. If the Government does not heed these warnings, then the responsibility is on its shoulders.
Another aspect of the approach of abandoning regulation is the over-all economics. The Government promises a sunny morning in a deregulated environment. It tells us that if we throw open the trucking industry to competition we are going to have a sunny day, the economy is going to boom and there will be more wealth created. However, the reality is quite different. The reality includes aspects of safety, the threat to jobs and a realistic look at what happens when we throw out regulation and leave the trucking industry to an open "Adam Smith" kind of economic environment. What we will have is a David and Goliath situation. David is the Canadian trucking industry and Goliath is the American trucking industry. What the Government is doing is not only putting David up against Goliath, but it is going to take away David's slingshot. It is going to leave David defenceless against the giant Goliath.
To illustrate, let me just say that the experience with deregulation in the trucking industry in the United States has been that large firms have gobbled up little trucking firms and there is increased concentration in the trucking industry. There are fewer firms dominating the market. We predict this will happen in Canada. We will have fewer and fewer large firms dominating the market and the little firms will go out of business and disappear.
At the same time, and this has actually started to happen, Canadians will have no barriers to Americans coming into the Canadian market while Americans continue to maintain significant barriers to the Canadian trucking industry entering into the American market. There is still competition legislation in the United States with which the trucking industry has to contend. In Canada we have very weak watered-down competition legislation. The structures of the American and Canadian industry work in favour of the American industry. There is a much larger population base in the United States and many more urban centres, so there is a vast network of communities which can be a strong base for a trucking industry, whereas in Canada there are only a few large cities
and our trade is spread out east to west. When it comes to facing competition in the north-south direction, we are going to be going up against a Goliath. With the Government taking away David's slingshot, we are in serious trouble. Therefore, the approach of abandoning regulation is a dangerous approach for Canadians.

Mr. Speaker, I would like to make three points about the decision of the Government to abandon the regulatory system for the trucking industry. This approach will increase the risk of accidents. In an unregulated environment and with open competition, there will be pressure on the truckers to work long hours until they become extremely tired, and tiredness can cause accidents. I have here figures which show that the number of accidents increases with tiredness, and these figures are contained in a document. I believe that an unregulated system will increase the danger of accidents.
In addition, the Manitoba Trucking Association has indicated that the approach taken by the federal Government will affect adversely many workers in Manitoba and that 10,000 jobs are involved in that province. This is therefore a major issue for Manitoba and I would like the Government to realize how this will jeopardize jobs in Manitoba. It is time that this Government realize that Manitoba exists. The Government should take care of the economy of Manitoba, not only of Central Canada. Mr. Speaker, I believe that you are indicating that I have only one minute left.

I would like to sum up by saying that the Government has chosen to abandon regulation, rather than taking the opposite approach, which would be to examine the present regime of regulation carefully and find out where this system could be improved. In that way we would take into consideration not only the present needs of the trucking industry but the needs of the shippers as well.
We in this Party would not take the position that there is no need for change since, obviously, even the trucking industry and the environment in which it operates changes, including what goes on in the United States industry. In the future we hope that the Government will bring in a regime that will be supportive of our trucking industry, one that will better serve the interests of the shippers as well.
Rather than abandoning regulation the Government should be seeking to improve it. I call upon the Government to back away from the approach of throwing out the baby with the bath water. It should take a constructive approach rather than be blinded by its own ideological commitment to the "Adam Smith" model of the free market.
I hope the Government will take into consideration some of the implications of the approach that I have noted in my remarks, including the questions of safety, the negative impact on the economy of Manitoba and just what type of ruthless
February 10, 1987

competition it will be putting the Canadian trucking industry up against without adequate protection.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subtopic: MOTOR VEHICLE TRANSPORT ACT, 1986 MEASURE TO ENACT
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to deal very briefly with the three major thrusts of the Hon. Member's speech and invite his response to the points I hope to make.
With respect to the question of abandoning regulation, the Hon. Member says that we have an ideological commitment to the free market. I take it that is in reference to the Regina Manifesto. It has been a long time since that resolution was passed by the Party which the New Democratic Party succeeds. The fact is we do not live in the 1930s anymore. We live in an increasingly competitive world economy. If the people of Winnipeg cannot get their goods to market then they will not have jobs, their children will not have jobs and the garment industry in Manitoba, for example, will not be able to get its products to wherever it is they are sent. More than 80 per cent of the goods produced in Manitoba are sent to the United States. Many of the Hon. Member's constituents work in the garment industry. If there is not an efficient trucking industry in place to get their products to market then their jobs will be less secure.
Transportation is a vitally important matter for the people of Winnipeg and for those from all parts of Canada. We are trying to do something to make the trucking industry more competitive and more efficient. I remind the Hon. Member that six major companies have their headquarters in Winnipeg.
The U.S. experience, which I mentioned, earlier was that employment increased by 22 per cent after deregulation in 1980 and that trucking employees were 40 per cent better paid than the average private sector employee. With respect to what the Hon. Member was saying about Canadians not being able to compete, does he not realize that Canadian truckers have increased their share of total transborder traffic by 8 per cent and 12 per cent between the years 1980 and 1984? We are able to compete in that market. There are approximately 1,000 Canadian trucking companies which now compete south of the border. We can and will compete. We must compete better.
The Hon. Member mentions the old cliche about regulations. I am told that the CTC publishes regulations virtually as fast as they can be printed. There is a regulation in place which tells railways what their tickets must look like, what size they should be and what type of print they should have. This is the type of nonsense and weight on peoples' backs from which we are trying to get away. We are trying to get away from needless regulations that prevent newcomers to the trucking industry from getting going and providing more vitality to an industry that is vital to Canada.
With respect to the question of safety, the Hon. Member for Bonaventure-Iles-de-la-Madeleine (Mr. Gray), as reported at page 3225 of Hansard for yesterday, spoke at length about the new uniform safety code. His points are summarized well at the bottom of that page. I assume the Hon. Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper) has not read the Hon.

There was clearly no agreement to completely deregulate the system after three years, or at any time, nor was there any consensus that the new entry standard was intended to be transitional only. That was not in the Memorandum of Understanding and there was no consensus on it among the provinces and the federal Government. However, the Bill contains automatic sunsetting on this new shifted burden of proof of entry regime which Clause 30 imposes.
As another example of violation of the Memorandum of Understanding between the provinces and the federal Government, Manitoba agreed to sign the understanding on the basis that an interested person would only have to demonstrate that the granting of the application would be potentially detrimental to the public interest. This legislation leaves out the word "potentially". The entry standards document which the council of Ministers adopted provided that an application could be opposed on the grounds that the applicant is unfit, unwilling or unable to operate the undertaking. The Bill has replaced the words "is unfit" with a different criterion. This is like throwing a deck of cards up in the air and hoping that they all land in proper order.
The Memorandum of Understanding used the words "economic or social development", but in the Bill we see "the economic or social development of Canada". Manitoba signed the Memorandum of Understanding on the understanding that the impact of a proposed service upon the economic and social
Motor Vehicule Transport Act, 1986
development of Manitoba would be considered by the transport board. The legislation leaves out such words as "or a province" or "or a region of Canada". Those words do not appear in the Bill.
Another area which violates the Memorandum of Understanding is with regard to the national definition of fitness recommended by the CCMTA. The legislation proposes that fitness certificates or licences issued by one jurisdiction to a carrier domiciled in that jurisdiction be recognized by other provinces. That would mean that a carrier which got a fitness certificate in one province could operate in any other province or territory and in the United States. Due to the wording of the Act, a provincial transport board which simply recognized a licence from another province and made no independent assessment of the carrier's fitness would likely be found by a court to be illegally fettering its discretion. One province could have very slack rules on the matter of the fitness and quality of trucks and equipment, on maintenance standard and procedures, and with regard to the number of hours which a driver may drive without rest. The province with the poorest fitness standards could issue a fitness certificate to a carrier who could then operate anywhere else in Canada without having to worry. A province which has good standards could do nothing about that under this legislation. That is another violation of the Memorandum of Understanding. So much for the sound and consultative federal-provincial relations. That is another example of the betrayal by the Government of an understanding which was signed by everyone.
Another issue is that of international trucking and our relations with the United States. There is today a Bill before the U.S. Senate which provides for the levying of heavy vehicle user taxes on all trucks which use the interstate highway system, which is partially financed by the federal authority in the United States. In the case of Canadian truckers, the additional tax will amount to some $700 per vehicle. There is no provision in Canada for an equivalent tax on U.S. trucks coming here. It is another sell-out of the worst kind. The Government is prepared to allow the U.S. trucking industry, which is massive compared to our industry, to come into this country. It will be allowed to operate in this country under a regime that Canadian trucking and railroad companies cannot have in the United States.
Those so-called Canadians sitting over there, sit back and quietly acquiesce to this kind of betrayal of our sovereignty and independence over transportation with the United States. I hope the Government will withdraw this legislation and wait until the national safety code is in place, until there is a national safety board that is functioning with the full agreement of the provinces, and there is a uniform national standard of safety, equipment, maintenance, and work rules that provide for the safer operation of the trucking industry. That should be in place before the Government deals with this legislation which violates a federal-provincial agreement.

February 10, 1987

Parliamentary Secretary agrees that the Senate in the United States has acted improperly, why not make a reciprocal provision in Canadian law that will serve notice on the U.S. administration and Congress that we will deal with their transporters coming to Canada in the same manner? The Parliamentary Secretary stated that there are some one million Canadians who work in industries that are dependent on transportation. It is in the worst interests of industry and businesses in Canada if we do not have a transportation system in all modes that is not only competitive, safe and efficient but also economically viable. speechtext:

speechtext:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise today to draw the attention of the House to the basic unfairness in the Canadian Wheat Board's recent statement that there would be no final payment on hard wheat sold during the 1985-86 crop year.
February 10, 1987

The growers who produced the higher quality wheat are particularly disadvantaged by this move, since the Canadian Wheat Board made a profit of S54 million on the sale of their wheat. Under the pooling system, this profit was transferred to reduce the loss incurred on the sale of lower grades.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the plight of Canada's hungry is reaching alarming proportions. They are becoming increasingly dependent upon the generosity of food banks across the country. Last year food banks served over 300,000 Canadians.

As a result of that, and flowing from that freedom of speech principle, there also comes some responsibility. One of the things that I think is absolutely fundamental to the whole business of parliamentary immunity is that we as Members are responsible for our actions and words in the House of Commons. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it seems evident that the Government is anxious to push Bill C-19 through Parliament with rather unseemly haste. I enter the debate to protest that action on the part of the Government.
Bill C-19, respecting the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986, replaces a very old Act of Parliament, one going back as far as 1953 or 1954. It is quite understandable that an Act of Parliament from the fifties needs to be altered, changed, and updated to meet the demands, requirements, and needs of the eighties, nineties, and into the next century. It probably is, in respect of the needs of the trucking industry, time for a change. However, if it is time for a change, surely Parliament needs time to consider fully all the implications, effects, results, and consequences of this change.
To move that the question be now put is a signal from government Members that they may know enough, or think they do, and that they may have heard enough or think they have. Perhaps they are sufficiently convinced about Bill C-19 to think that no more debate is required. However, Hon. Members of Parliament on this side of the House are saying that that is not so, that we need more time to consider, reflect, examine, and debate the principles of the Bill.
I remind Hon. Members that the Canadian Trucking Association decided it was time to take a new look at the position of the industry regarding motor carrier regulatory
February 10, 1987

reform sometime ago, and it took them a lot of time to arrive at a new policy. In fact, Bill C-19 reflects the culmination of a full three years of tug of war among different interests-the shippers, the truckers, and the Government. It took three years to achieve the policy goals which are now reflected in part in Bill C-19, yet the House began to consider Bill C-19 only last Thursday. On Monday, the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Government House Leader, speaking for the Government, rose in his place after speaking for four minutes to move that the question be now put. Does it strike you, Sir, as being fair that we should be allowed one hour and 28 minutes to debate a Bill whose policy took three years to develop, three years to consider an important issue that has not been changed since the 1950s?
I must make a plea to you, Sir, and to all Hon. Members: we need more time too. Take the pressure off. This House is not a rubber stamp nor is it a sausage factory that drives out Bills on an assembly line. When arguments like mine are made, some Hon. Members say that we should let the Bill go to committee where it can receive in depth treatment and perhaps even be amended. There will be a time, of course, when this Bill will go to committee, but in my view it should not go to committee until its principles are fully understood, fully comprehended and fully appreciated or rejected by the House.
We call second reading of a Bill a routine proceeding, but it should never be so routine that when a major shift in policy occurs and when a new direction is charted, we should not have the time to debate it. I am not opposed to the charting of new courses, far from it, but surely we as parliamentarians must not deal with the underlying principles of the Bill in some kind of a routine, reflective, hurried or pressured fashion. Is it unreasonable for me to propose that, Sir?
Parliaments go back to the time of the Anglo-Saxon kings. Even though they were not as representative as Parliaments are today, we know that the earliest of Parliaments saw themselves as being supreme legislative, administrative and judicial assemblies, and no ancient British king would attempt to legislate without the advice and approval of that assembly. All I am saying is that we need time to consider this Bill. We must remind ourselves in asking for that time that this honourable House has very ancient foundations.
The Crown today is the executive branch of Government, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and his Ministers. However, any Member of Parliament may rise to tell the executive branch that it is not to be allowed to take Parliament for granted or to abuse its rights and privileges. Paramount among those rights is the right to debate fully important pieces of legislation such as Bill C-19. I ask you, Sir, does it not sound rather abusive to you to have the first day of debate last Thursday and then on Monday to have an Hon. Member move that the question now be put? It sounds abusive to me.
By putting this motion forward, the Government is preventing a major decision of Parliament from being at least
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
considered. I would like to explain what that major decision could have been, not that it would have been taken by Parliament but at least it could have been considered. That decision is that this Bill be not now read a second time but that it be read a second time six months hence. It is no longer possible to move such a motion. We have been excluded from putting before Parliament that possibility.
A Bill based on a new policy approach which took a full three years to develop by the industry, its clients and the Government working together to replace a policy that goes back as far as the 1950s may very well require at least six months of study. During the February recess of Parliament and the Easter break, we may very well want to talk to shippers and truckers in our regions to ask them if Bill C-19 as they understand it does what they hope it will do. There is very good evidence to suggest that Bill C-19 does not fit the bill of fare and that the degree of consensus that was reached after three years leaves much to be desired, at least insofar as that consensus has been translated into legislation.
The Canadian Trucking Association recently took another very careful look at its position, the position it reached after three years of active consideration. It went through some very serious soul searching and concluded that Bill C-19 is a disaster in terms of a meaningful transitional approach to regulatory reform. It concluded that Bill C-19 does not meet any of the industry's primary concerns. At first the industry thought it did but now it sees that it does not.
The message is clear. This question should not now be put. It should be debated and debated more, and perhaps it should even be set aside for a short period of time. Surely a Government which is as shaky, inexperienced and insecure as this one would not want to force upon the trucking industry an ill-considered package of reforms which may not achieve what is hoped for. There is no disagreement on this side of the House about what is hoped for. What is hoped for is an easy, helpful passage from the excessive regulation we have had in the past to full deregulation. However, we cannot do that without much careful thought.
Would the Government really want to push through this House a Bill which could very well give U.S. truckers an important competitive advantage over Canadian truckers? The U.S. trucking industry already enjoys certain advantages because of U.S. tax reform which we do not have yet and because of lower fuel taxes. Despite Bill C-19 which is now being pushed at us, the industry has already drawn up a new policy position. Parliament needs time to consider that new policy position, so the question should not now be put. We should consider more carefully what has taken place in very recent weeks and days.
The industry is convinced, for example, that Bill C-19, in bringing in a totally new test, will lead to a deluge of early applications. This will swamp the process even before it has been fully tested. The industry is convinced that there will be numerous court challenges drawn out of Bill C-19, and the industry is concerned about problems associated with safety.

Hon. Members will know that in the U.S. motor carrier regulatory reform concerned itself mainly with the economic aspects. As important as they are, the U.S. failed to consider the safety aspects in a comprehensive manner at the same time. They are now paying the price. If we fully deregulate by January 1, 1988, will a new and comprehensive national safety code also be in effect? I doubt it, but Members of Parliament want an answer to that question. No, I say to you that after only one hour and 20 minutes of debate, after only six speakers from this side of the House, it is not the time to move that the question now be put. Following that, rather than sending it to a committee, we may want to put it aside for six months so that Parliament can keep up with developments in this important public policy area.
The industry believes its concerns could possibly be satisfied if Bill C-19 were amended in certain clauses. Particularly bothersome to them is Clause 7. The parliamentary committee which examined the Government's document Freedom to Move made certain recommendations. Let me deal with but one area where committee members made recommendations. For example, the committee said that the international aspect of trucking should be treated somewhat differently from the domestic. Nowhere in Bill C-19 will you find that recommendation incorporated. The question should not now be put. We should know why that recommendation was rejected. The Bill calls for deregulation in the trucking industry by January 1, 1988. Many of the provinces, led as they often are by Ontario with two-thirds of the trucking market, want a longer period, up to five years, before the industry is totally deregulated. If they want such a period of grace, I ask all Hon. Members and the Government, why should the question now be put? speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am glad to rise to participate in this debate on Bill C-18 with regard to the fundamental reform of transportation in this country. I listened with a great deal of interest to my friend,

February 10, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
the Hon. Member for Cochrane-Superior (Mr. Penner). I was prompted to rise today because the Member for Cochrane-Superior is one of the more respected Members of this House. He has many years of experience and, at one time in his career, was Chairman of the Canadian Parliamentary Association. In that capacity he was able to visit England from time to time and see the mother of parliaments at work.
He is one of the more restrained Members on the opposition side in terms of rhetoric. He very rarely indulges in hyperbole. He is not like the more dramatic Member for Gander- Twillingate (Mr. Baker) who has been resurrected in opposition. He was quiet as a church mouse at a communion Christmas for years in Government, but has really come alive in opposition with his scintillating questions and sometimes interesting contributions to debate. This is almost a second life for the Hon. Member for Gander-Twillingate. The Member for Cochrane-Superior is pretty consistent and thorough and fairly steadfast.
I am Chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport to which Bill C-19 will, depending upon the will of the House, eventually be referred. Bill C-18 is already before the committee. Being an objective and non-partisan chairman, I am not going to get into the fundamental issues with which that committee will deal. I was, however, rather bothered by a couple of the comments of my hon. friend for Cochrane- Superior. I will develop the chronology of the time taken for debate on Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 and comment on the perhaps unintentional insult by the Hon. Member who is a member of the standing committee.
The Member suggested that because this Bill received second reading in the House there will be no change made to it in committee. As all Hon. Members know, as a new Government we may have had some problems and made some mistakes. However, in this new Parliament there has been a consistent desire for fundamental parliamentary reform from the top to the bottom, including in committee work. I am not going to debate all the areas of parliamentary reform, but for the Hon. Member to suggest that passage of second reading in the House means that the Bill will not be changed in committee flies in the face of his conviction and that of all members who support parliamentary reform.
The Government wants this Bill to be moved from the floor of the House into committee where the meaningful work, with respect, will be done through the presentation of briefs, the hearing of evidence and, based on that evidence, the submission of meaningful recommendations for change. After all, in its report Freedom to Move the committee produced the report entitled: Change, Choice and Challenge.
1 agree with members opposite and members on the government side that there are presently aspects of this Bill which must be examined very closely. Members on both sides have pointed out areas in which there should be change when the Bill reaches committee. There will not be one thing changed in the House. There has not been one new argument on this issue since the debate began.
Let us get down to the facts and not stir up a myth that this Bill is being forced through the House. Debates which continue day after day in which everything is repeated ad nauseam turn the public off. The public is not educated by that. Meaningful work in committee will educate the public. My friend knows that the longest debate in the British House of Commons in recent history was a two-day debate on the admission of England to the European Common Market.
With respect to debate on these two Bills, admittedly the Minister of Transport (Mr. Crosbie) spoke for part of the day on Friday, December 19. Debate on Bill C-18 was launched on December 19 before the House recessed for Christmas. We resumed the debate when the House reconvened on January 19. The opposition spokesman spoke for a meaningful part of that day. Following the debate on the softwood lumber legislation, we resumed debate on January 27, 28, 29 and 30, as well as on Monday, February 2 and Tuesday, February 3 when there was a motion to extend the hours. The question was finally put early on Wednesday morning.
As the chairman of the committee considering this legislation, let me state candidly that I did not see the necessity to extend hours until four o'clock in the morning in order to put the question. While it was an interesting debate, until that time there had not been a deliberate attempt by the Opposition to prevent the second reading of the legislation. However, the fact is that there had been eight days of debate on Bill C-18. Admittedly, some were not full days of debate.

closure on Bills. I suggest that the public resents Bills being debated ad nauseam in this Chamber, when the real work is essentially done in committees.
We want this Bill to go to committee, but the Opposition cannot complain about its being forced through Parliament. There have been three days on which to debate Bill C-19, but on each of those days there was a concurrence motion by the Opposition. That uses the time for the debate on the principles of Bill C-19. Obviously, the Government House Leader would feel thwarted because the opposition tactics were more than retaliation to the extended hours on Tuesday, February 3.
Perhaps I am being too frank in admitting that I thought debate on Bill C-18 was proceeding smoothly. I was a Member of Parliament at that time, and I am glad to see the Hon. Member for Regina West (Mr. Benjamin) in the House because I heard him refer to that previous great national debate on transport.
When I heard Members speak about the time it took to put Bill C-18 through the formal second reading phase, I referred to Hansard of 1966 and 1967 and the debate on Bill C-231, which was the then National Transportation Bill introduced by the then Minister of Transport, Mr. Pickersgill. That Bill was introduced for first reading on August 29, 1966. Second reading debate began on September 1; debate resumed on September 6 and September 7, and the question was put on September 8. There were four days of second reading debate on Bill C-231, the predecessor to the transportation legislation we are debating today. That vote referred the Bill to the Transport and Communications Committee. The next sitting was not until October 2, due to a parliamentary recess, and the committee eventually reported the Bill on December 6, 1966. During that period from October 6 to December 6, there were

The fact is we have taken parts of the whole eight days on debate on Bill C-18 and we had three days slotted for Bill C-19. There were motions to concur and we were into debate on Monday, February 9, and today. In total, there have been 13 days devoted to Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 and we still have not finished. Twenty years ago they finished in four days. That certainly is an indication of why the Government House Leader can get a little impatient. All Hon. Members who were involved in transport, especially the Hon. Member for Regina West, is aware that the issues in this matter have been around for years. This Bill was not snuck in under cover of darkness so that it caught the Opposition by surprise.
The then Minister of Transport, the now Deputy Prime Minister (Mr. Mazankowski), in a memorable speech on February 21, 1985, set out the parameters of reform to the transportation sector of which he wanted Canadians to be aware and respond to. That speech was really the manifesto of this Bill. The gestation period was not carried on behind closed doors. It was done in the public domain, in the light of day. The then Minister of Transport threw out the challenge to Canadians on February 21, 1985, and we are now into 1987. There were consultations after his speech and, finally, on July 15, 1985, the Minister released his Freedom to Move paper, which was the consolidation of many of the things he had heard from interested parties. That Freedom to Move paper was released publicly on July 15, 1985, so that again the public could be involved and they could see how the Minister of the day had distilled the public input and they could see where we were going with the impending legislation. The Freedom to Move paper was not sent back to the bureaucracy behind closed doors. It was referred to the Standing Committee on Transport in October or November of 1985 and the standing

February 10, 1987

committee had hearings across the country. We did not go to every place but we certainly had hearings in Ottawa, Vancouver, Winnipeg and Halifax. We heard from 95 organizations and received 152 submissions in a very active two-month period.
We then perused our report and reported back on our Freedom to Move paper in December. We then went to the North in the spring of 1986, and in June 26, 1986, the Bill was tabled. We then went home for the summer, and the Bill percolated in the public domain. Again there were representations, submissions and consultations. In the new Parliament on November 4, 1986, the Bill came back and, as I mentioned earlier, the present Minister of Transport made the initial speech on December 19, just before we adjourned for Christmas.
I just cannot get too excited, as even the most objective chairman, to the charges from the Opposition that this Bill is being rushed through in unholy haste when the previous Bill, in a Parliament 20 years ago, took four days on second reading. Mr. Speaker, I wish the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) had not taken so long to respond to the questions of my hon. friend. I wanted to ask him the following question in his capacity as Chairman of the Transport Committee. What does he need to make a commitment that the committee will in fact travel? This is a critical piece of information.
I remind the Hon. Member that he reminded us of the length of debate when a similar matter was discussed some time ago. That was after a royal commission had studied the matter for more than one year. No royal commission has

February 10, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
studied the matter which is now before us. As a matter of fact, there has been a document produced entitled Freedom to Move. Some people felt that this put down the framework for transportation regulation upgrading for the next few decades and that it would be appropriate to take this document to the people of Canada and hold hearings on it. That is what governments have done over the years on critical matters such as this. In years past governments have actually given matters such as this to royal commissions to travel with around the country and hold dozens and dozens of hearings in every province and every territory and every major metropolitan area. But what did the Government do when it had the opportunity to show how committed it was to receiving public input?
I ask the Chairman of the Transport Committee: Did the committee travel across Canada and hold open public hearings? Well, technically, yes, it did. It held hearings in three centres other than in the capital city. It ignored seven of the 10 provinces of Canada and both of the territories of Canada. In other words, most of Canada was blanked out by the committee. Were the hearings held in two of the largest metropolitan cities in North America and the two largest metropolitan cities in Canada, Montreal and Toronto? No. When a concerned and effective Opposition looks at the track record of the Government to see how committed it is to receiving decent input from those who will be most affected by this legislation, I have to say to the Chairman of the Transport Committee that the track record looks very poor. There has been no indication that the Government is actually serious if we consider the precedents that we have seen thus far.
On many occasions in my position as House Leader for the New Democratic Party I have asked the Government House Leader and his Parliamentary Secretary if the Transport Committee is prepared to travel. After weeks and weeks of asking this same question I have received no answer. Based on what I have seen the Government do in terms of its willingness to travel on critical pieces of legislation, I must say that I do not have any confidence that the Government is serious at this point.
The Chairman of the Transport Committee is a man for whom I have a great deal of respect. He has indicated that we have been dragging out this debate. I want to remind the Hon. Member that I am but the fourth speaker from the New Democratic Party to speak on legislation that will touch every part of Canada, every resource sector and every major manufacturing company in the country.
To give Hon. Members an idea of the scale of the operation we are discussing today, I looked back to see to what extent this industry touches the lives of Canadians. How large an industry is it? If one considers just the for-hire trucking companies, I found out that in 1982, the last time we had a specific figure for the number of trucks and tractors for for-hire trucking, the figure came to 50,600, with an additional 83,000 trailers and other related equipment. That is a massive operation, and that is the for-hire trucking only. The private
trucking firms with their own subsidiaries have 481,000 trucks and tractors and another 83,000 trailers. That does not include the hundreds of companies that move household goods across the country or within large metropolitan areas. This massive undertaking includes hundreds of thousands of trucks moving goods in excess of $6 billion in terms of gross operating revenue.
Surely the Chairman of the Standing Committee on Transport does not feel that having four or five speakers from a political Party is excessive. Surely in his position as Chairman of the Transport Committee he does not think it is unreasonable to entertain the idea of travelling and holding hearings in critical parts of the country. Yet no answers have been received. It perplexes and concerns us, and it makes us feel that perhaps the Government is less than serious about giving sufficient opportunity for the people to be heard who will be most affected by this Bill, and its associate Bill C-18, the deregulation of the transportation industry generally.
At the end of my short presentation during the question and answer period, perhaps the Chairman will take that opportunity to indicate to the House, and to the people of Canada who are concerned about this matter, what his intentions are with regard to receiving input on this critical issue through open hearings in different parts of Canada.
My colleague, the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay- Atikokan (Mr. Angus), made an excellent point in the introduction to his speech last Thursday when this debate started. He indicated that often there is an association with what is happening in our trucking industry in terms of reregulation with what has happened in the United States. This recognizes that over the past few years the United States has gone through the process of reregulation. Yet it is folly to compare what happened in the United States with what happens in Canada. When the United States changed and reregulated its trucking industry, it knew that in the northern part of its country there is a country called Canada which had a relatively insignificant transportation industry relative to that of the United States. It is quite a different matter for Canada. The boundary between Canada and the United States is the longest undefended boundary in the world. When we open it up and welcome American carriers carte blanche, we are inviting a giant into our household. Their ability to move in and take over from existing Canadian systems is obvious. It is inappropriate to compare what has happened in the United States with what is happening in Canada, and assume that what has transpired since the introduction of reregulation will be the same in both countries.
I wish to focus on a number of critical points. Of course, one of them is safety. A number of representatives of the Government, particularly the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Kilgour) has mentioned that there will be a made-in-Canada national safety code that will be in place to bring some comfort. We all agree that if the trucking industry
February 10, 1987

is to be deregulated, many of us have raised concerns that this may mean that the highways will be less safe. Does it mean that trucking companies will be pushed beyond the endurance of their drivers and the reasonable safety of their vehicles? One might ask if we have evidence to suggest that. I say that we have a considerable amount of evidence.
A recent study, which was funded by the American trucking companies, found that about 60 per cent of all the heavy truck accidents involved a fatigued truck driver. The comprehensive study of 231 accidents in six western states involved 39 fatal accidents which claimed the lives of 16 truck occupants and 33 occupants of other vehicles.
The study goes on to state that:
The surprisingly high percentage of fatigue-related accidents is three times greater than actually reported on the regular accident report forms. A fatigue-related accident was determined when the truck operator drove more than 16 or more consecutive hours per trip.
It is incredible to think that truck drivers would be expected to be responsible for a major rig on the highway for a period in excess of 16 hours. It is not surprising that fatigue would settle in and danger on our highways would be the result.
The report further states:
One-half of all the truck accidents studied were single vehicle accidents. The second most serious cause of truck accidents was mechanical failure (18 per cent). However, of all mechanical failure accidents, 63 per cent also involved driver fatigue. Thus, fatigue probably prevented the professional drivers from possibly overcoming or safely reacting to a mechanical failure.
The report further states:
Fatigue accidents are reported to result from deliberate violations of hours of service by truck drivers.
The operative term there is "deliberate violations of hours of service by truck drivers". The report further states:
One out of every three heavy truck drivers on the highways is estimated to be driving beyond 10 hour per day standard recommended by the Bureau of Motor Carrier Safety. It was also estimated that 6.5 per cent of all heavy truck drivers are driving more than 15 consecutive hours per trip. A small percentage, but if extrapolated to 1.2 million heavy truck drivers on the highway, this is a sizable figure warned the AAA Foundation for Traffic Safety.
It is no secret that one of the spin-offs of the process of deregulation of the trucking industry will be to bring a great deal more competition to our highways. At first glance I suspect that people will say that this is obviously in the best interest of shippers, the Canadian economy, and that it is good news for us all.
The result of this enhanced competition will mean that large, small, and medium-sized trucking companies will be pushing and cutting back on maintenance costs, and perhaps on the concern that they have for their drivers. It is for this reason that we are particularly concerned when the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport states that a made-in-Canada national safety code will be put in place.
In looking at the situation that was in effect in November of last year, for example, the safety initiatives that include the procedure for audit of employers' records, I notice that the Canadian Trucking Association's position is still to be
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
developed. The National Council of the Motor Transportation Authority also states that the procedure is still to be developed. The position of the Canadian Trucking Association and the CCMTA is that the policy for record systems for operator profile or driver profile still has to be developed. I also consider such things as the Interprovincial Record Exchange, and find that that also has to be developed in terms of the view of the Canadian Transport Association, and similarly with the CCMTA which says it still has to be developed.
The only conclusion that can be drawn is that these safety codes and the understandings, which would result in enhanced safety as a result of deregulation, will be determined sometime in the future. They will not necessarily be determined this year, because the dates here indicate the year 1989. We are concerned about these situations when they are brought to our attention. Why does it appear that the Government is so intent on getting this Bill into committee and back into the House of Commons and passed into legislation prior to real consideration being given to the safety factor? I have here a letter that was recently written by the Minister of Highways and Transportation in the Province of Manitoba to the Minister of Transport in Ottawa. In the second paragraph it states that, "I remain of the view that the Bill is seriously flawed and constitutes a breach of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding on the reform of extra-provincial trucking regulation agreed upon by your predecessor and all provincial and territorial transport Ministers on February 27, 1985."
This raises some serious concerns. Does it mean that once again when it comes to provincial-federal government dealings there seems to have been a breakdown? Here is a Minister responsible for the highways in one of Canada's western provinces saying that in his view the Bill is not only seriously flawed, but also constitutes a breach of the terms of the Memorandum of Understanding that the province and the federal Government had entered into. Then he went on to explain it in some detail. Quite frankly they were quite complicated details upon which I am not in a position to expand. Presumably more learned Members of the House will be able to explain them when the Bill is before the Standing Committee on Transport. I simply use them to point out that again there seems to have been a breakdown in co-operation between the federal Government and the appropriate provincial Government.
Over the course of this very short debate some people have asked why New Democrats seem hesitant about rapid passage of Bill C-19 and why we are listing our concerns very carefully at second reading stage.
I asked myself, as a Member of Parliament, the following question: Who opposes the Bill and who supports it? At the top of the list of organizations opposing the legislation in its present form-and I emphasize that because I assume we can make significant improvements-is the Canadian Trucking Association. If this piece of legislation had been thoughtfully

February 10, 1987
Motor Vehicle Transport Act, 1986
designed and drafted, after appropriate consultation, to improve the lot of transport in Canada, I do not think it would be surprising that the Canadian Trucking Association would support it. However, that Association is opposed to it. I also notice that provincial transport associations are opposed, as is the Province of Manitoba. Other provinces have indicated serious doubts once they had a chance to look at some of the fine points in the legislation. Perhaps that is one of the reasons the Government has decided to proceed with some haste in terms of getting through the legislation. When I find out that all major participants oppose it, I suspect there is a lot more here than what simply meets our eyes as parliamentarians.
I should like to refer to a November article which appeared in The Globe and Mail in which it was reported that United States trucking companies were expecting that Canadian trucking deregulation would mean a continental bonanza by giving them unrestricted access to the Canadian market, thus allowing them to offer non-stop Los Angeles to Vancouver or Miami to Toronto service. The article went on to note that one area where United States carriers were expected to make inroads was in the business currently going to private carriers. In 1984, Canadian companies did about $5 billion worth of business with their private fleets, but with rates falling they could be encouraged to shift to the four higher carriers. United States carriers also expect to take business away from Canadians by signing deals with U.S. parent companies to transport the goods of the parent and its Canadian subsidiary.
We are a Party which has always been concerned about the extremely high level of foreign ownership of our economy, particularly our manufacturing economy, as well as the cash flows and dividend flows which move out of the country as a result of subsidiary branch plant economy in Canada. We now find that trucking companies in the United States will take advantage of the parent company being in the United States and a subsidiary being in Canada to lock up, in a sense, the movement of goods back and forth between the parent and the subsidiary by using their own trucking companies, thereby using American trucking companies.
Mr. Cope, Executive Vice-President of the Ontario Trucking Association, indicated that that would settle the fate of a lot of things in Canada without Canadian companies getting a kick at the cat. This individual in charge of a trucking association in Canada's industrial heartland is concerned that American companies will have advantages which will not exist for Canadian companies.
The end result of the process will inevitably be concentration of ownership in the trucking business. That is what happened in the United States. The Executive Director of the U.S. Independent Truck Owners and Operators Association, a strong proponent of deregulation prior to 1980, testified before congressional oversight hearings in 1983 and said that the effects of the Motor Carrier Act, 1980 on the trucking industry and labour force had been disastrous. The process of deregulation in the United States has been disastrous, in his terms. Both the truck load and the LTL sectors were ravaged
by deregulation, with medium-sized carriers forced out of business through the destructive practices engaged by large carriers through the use of discounting tactics. He cited studies which predicted that after the initial shake-up of the industry had been completed there would be four or five giant nationwide LTL carriers, approximately 20 medium-sized regional LTL carriers, and little else.
It is one more step in the process toward more concentration of the economy being in the hands of fewer players. If the Bill is designed to assist small Canadian trucking companies, and knowing that the experience in the U.S. has resulted in large multinational trucking companies becoming dominant in the market-place, it is fair to think that Bill C-19 is not in the best interests of small Canadian carriers.
I encourage the Government and the Parliamentary Secretary to give the matter a great deal of thought when it reaches committee stage, at which point we will have a chance to bring forward appropriate witnesses to indicate, from their point of view, the effects of the legislation on them.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to take part in the debate on this motion which I would like to read once more to the House:
That, in the opinion of this House, the Government should consider the advisability of honouring the memory of the Right Honourable Lester B. Pearson by commissioning a statue of him to be placed on Parliament Hill.
The Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes), my colleagues of the majority party and myself support wholeheartedly the notion of commissioning a statue to honour the memory of this illustrious Canadian. On January 19, the last time this motion was debated in the House, there was a slight misunderstanding as concerns the position of the members of the majority. I believe that this has now been cleared up and that my hon. friends opposite have had an opportunity to examine the report on statues honouring prime ministers of Canada and other commemorative works, which the Hon. Member for Simcoe North (Mr. Lewis) tabled on behalf of the Minister today.
Mr. Speaker, as the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) has himself pointed out, he requested this report last fall because, in his opinion, an analysis of the policy and the tradition for such works could assist Parliamentarians in the examination of future commemorative projects, especially statues on Parliament Hill. As no new statue had been erected on Parliament Hill for many years, the experience acquired recently in the successful project to erect a statue honouring the memory of Prime Minister Diefenbaker was also an excellent opportunity to initiate a new process for such projects and make an objective examination of the existing situation.
One of the complaints most commonly heard is that often necessary information is not available to Parliament to make enlightened decisions concerning issues it is sometimes called upon to deal unexpectedly. The report tabled by the Minister of Public Works provides information, observations, useful data which, in my opinion at least, deserve our full attention.
Mr. Speaker, we must deal with the motion moved by the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I have every intention to support his motion as moved, if such is the desire of Hon. Members opposite. Partisanship should not enter into the consideration of a motion of this kind. The government Members have never intended to stoop to such low tactics.
In view of the information now available, I believe, however, that Mr. Pearson would be bestowed an honour still more worthy of his name if, during the next few weeks, we took the time to ponder upon all the aspects of this project of a commemorative statue. This is not an attempt at delaying or filibustering this project; quite the contrary, as you will see today. However, it is intented rather to consider the matter with all necessary information available for the best possible results.
One of the first points to consider is that Prime Minister St. Laurent's statue was erected, at Prime Minister Trudeau's, own suggestion in front of the Supreme Court building rather than on Parliament Hill. The selection of that particular location is obvious in view of Mr. St. Laurent's fame as a jurist, lawyer, law professor, president of the Quebec Bar and Minister of Justice. Prime Minister Trudeau did not feel at the time, I am sure, that the Supreme Court location was any less prestigious than any other spot on Parliament Hill. He had no
February 10, 1987

intention either, I am sure, of showing disrespect for the late Mr. St. Laurent who was universally cherished.
Mr. Speaker, Mr. Pearson had enjoyed a long and prestigious career as a diplomat, first as Under Secretary, and then as Secretary of State for External Affairs. He was also awarded the Nobel Peace Prize because of his immense contribution to world peace and prosperity after World War II. In view of Mr. Pearson's career and the consequent tribute paid to Mr. St. Laurent, I urge Hon. Members opposite to reconsider the idea of dealing rapidly with the motion to put the statue right on Parliament Hill, exclusively. Pearson Building for instance, the headquarters of the Department of External Affairs which is so capably headed by the Right Hon. Joe Clark.
Mr. Speaker, this is only one example of the aspects we should be looking at. It would seem normal to me that Hon. -were added to the motion for the obvious reasons I just mentioned. The decision remains with the sponsor, who is here in this House. speakeroldname: Mrs. Pauline Browes (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of the Environment):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of the Environment
subtopic: PRIVATE MEMBERS' BUSINESS-MOTIONS   RIGHT HONOURABLE LESTER B. PEARSON STATUE TO HONOUR HIS MEMORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to join in this debate on the motion of the Hon. Member for Glengarry- Prescott-Russell (Mr. Boudria). I am pleased to have this opportunity because this motion follows on the motion I introduced just two years ago to erect a statue in honour of John Diefenbaker on Parliament Hill. John Diefenbaker and Lester Pearson were great political rivals. Their debates here
Parliament Hill
on the floor of the House of Commons and across Canada on the campaign trail form a lively and colourful part of our nation's history. Their rivalry touched almost every aspect of our politics, Parliament and society. I am told that it even extended to who caught the largest fish in Lake Harrington. As all members know, of course, Lester Pearson was never able to match the four and a half pound trout which Mr. Diefenbaker caught. However, I must say there is a silly but persistent rumour that Mr. Diefenbaker never actually pulled the fish into the boat.
Lester Pearson's outlook on life was profoundly shaped by his upbringing in a religious family, in a manse, his service during the war and his experience as a diplomat. He held a firm belief that Canada could become a great nation, and his efforts as Prime Minister are a great testament to that conviction. His outstanding international experience is widely known. He is perhaps one of the very few Canadians to ever participate in both the League of Nations and the United Nations. He was Canada's Ambassador to the U.S., President of the UN General Assembly, winner of the Nobel Peace Prize, and Canadian Minister of External Affairs. He received over 24 honorary degrees and was known world-wide as a conciliator, and a passionate defender of the peace.
Although he never won a majority Government in the House of Commons, Lester Pearson's record as Prime Minister is remarkable. He established the Canada Pension Plan, the Canada Assistance Program, medicare, a new labour code, a new Bank Act, the Order of Canada, and of course a new flag. His years in office were a time of great change and progress for all Canadians.
Two years ago this month I introduced a private motion to have a statue of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker commissioned and placed on Parliament Hill. Subsequently the site for that statue was chosen and the world-renowned artist, Leo Mol, was selected to do the work. Last September 18, some 18 months after the motion was first introduced, the statue was unveiled on a brilliant day here on Parliament Hill. Thousands of Canadians from all parts of the country attended that ceremony.
The committee which established the Diefenbaker statue demonstrated that a coherent and consistent process for the provision of such statues can work and is needed. With the outstanding contributions of the Hon. Member for Saskatoon East (Mr. Ravis), Senator David Walker from Toronto, who was the Minister of Public Works in the Diefenbaker Government, and representatives from the Ministry of Public Works, the Department of the Secretary of State, the NCC, and the Speaker's office, we initiated a process which could end the ad hoc approach which has been used for these memorials.
That was precisely the purpose of my motion. It was not my intention to encourage further Private Members' Motions which would simply tread on ground we have already covered. Rather, I introduced the motion to alert Parliament to the
3310

February 10, 1987
Parliament Hill
problem of how we honour great Canadians like John Diefen-baker and Lester Pearson.
Since John A. Macdonald first recommended a statue in honour of George-Etienne Cartier in 1873, we have never followed a coherent process for statue commemoration. In fact, a motion such as mine had not been considered by Parliament for nearly 20 years because of the disastrous handling of the last two statues which were erected on Parliament Hill. In 1966, the then Secretary of State proposed that statues of four Prime Ministers be commissioned and placed on Parliament Hill. After a year of controversy and conflict, only two of the four statues were completed. The statue of the Hon. Arthur Meighen was placed in storage and is still there. The maquette for the statue of the Hon. R. B. Bennett was lost. All we have are some pictures of the maquette which are not acceptable.
For the next 20 years no action was taken to erect a statue for any other former Prime Minister. That is a sad commentary on the state of how we recognize our national leaders and celebrate our nation's history. When I first proposed my motion I wanted to address this inaction and encourage the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Mclnnes) to initiate a consistent statue policy. The days of a motion by motion approach to honouring former Prime Ministers must end or it will take us another 20 years just to erect statues for the eight Prime Ministers who have yet to be recognized.
I was pleased that the Minister of Public Works tabled in the House today the report on commemorative statues to Canadian Prime Ministers and commemoratives to other eminent Canadians. Included in the report is a section on how other countries pay tribute to their founders. Perhaps it is time we considered a national statuary hall similar to the one in the United States capital where each province would be allowed to honour its historic figures.
We have the report filed by the Minister and it is now time we started working together to consider these guidelines, instead of further ad hoc measures, in order that John Diefenbaker, Lester Pearson and all our former Prime Ministers can live in lasting memory here on Parliament Hill and in the National Capital Region as well as in our history books.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thought there would be general agreement by all Parties to pass this motion immediately. The Hon. Member for Lasalle (Mr. Lanthier) indicated that if the mover of the motion were in agreement, he would like the motion to be amended to include "other suitable sites" for the placement of a statue commemorating the Hon. Lester B. Pearson, but that if Parliament were in agreement, he would be prepared to accept the motion as it now stands. The Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre (Mrs. Browes) is indicating that she as well would agree to accept the motion as it is. I am very glad that Hon. Members opposite are prepared to accept this motion.
I want to say only a few words on this matter. I believe there should be a committee responsible for the placement of statues and other memorabilia on the Hill. I hope that such a committee would consider other distinguished parliamentarians who ought to be honoured. Two such parliamentarians come readily to mind, the first being the first Leader of the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation, which subsequently became the New Democratic Party, J.F. Woodsworth. I think members would also agree that the first woman M.P., Agnes Macphail, should be honoured at some time. I agree that after this Bill is passed, parliamentarians should have a good discussion on the matters which have been raised by my hon. friend.
As my colleagues, the Member for Prince Albert (Mr. Hovdebo) and the Member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Keeper), submitted, I think it is entirely appropriate to pass the motion of the Hon. Member for Glengarry-Prescott- Russell (Mr. Boudria) to ensure that a statue of Mike Pearson is placed on Parliament Hill. I was alive and well, and for part of the time even in this House, when the two great gladiators on the Canadian scene were John Diefenbaker and Mike Pearson. They were dominant figures for over a decade and had many battles. In recent Canadian history it is unusual for two such figures to be face to face for that length of time. For that reason alone, one may like to see them face to face on Parliament Hill.
It was agreed last year, through the passage of the motion of the Hon. Member for Scarborough Centre, that we would commemorate a statue to the memory of the Right Hon. John George Diefenbaker. All Parties agreed to that. I cannot say strongly enough how important it is to have a statue of the Right Hon. Mike Pearson on Parliament Hill as well. It may be necessary to relocate some statues, but there is still room on the Hill. Even the statue of Mr. Diefenbaker could be relocated, but it should remain on Parliament Hill. His great opponent should be located nearby, so they may face each other on the Hill.
I think we all agree on Mr. Pearson's great contributions, although a few have not been mentioned. One of his very great contributions was the development of a spirit of co-operative federalism. Quite frankly, in my opinion he understood Quebec even better than his successor. He established the Bilingualism and Biculturalism Royal Commission. I believe he was the first Prime Minister to be really concerned about election expenses. The Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson did make the proposal to establish the commission on which M. J. Coldwell, among others, served, to examine electoral expenses and contributions to Parties. That is a landmark which we sometimes forget to acknowledge.
In conclusion, I support the motion and I am encouraged by the remarks of our friends opposite today that while they may favour a somewhat different motion, they will support the
February 10, 1987

erection of a statue on Parliament Hill in honour of the Right Hon. Lester B. Pearson.
